name: GitLab Inc.
origin_detail: Started as an open-source project by Dmitriy Zaporozhets (with Valery Sizov) in Kharkiv, Ukraine, in Oct 2011; Sytse Sijbrandij joined to build a business: GitLab B.V. (Netherlands) 2013, GitLab Inc. 2014, Y Combinator W15; all-remote, incorporated in the US
openness_notes: Began as a fully MIT-licensed project (2011-2013). Since the Enterprise Edition split (GitLab 6.0, Aug 2013) it is explicitly open core: Community Edition is MIT, while EE features are under the proprietary 'GitLab EE licence' (source-available, not open source); SaaS (GitLab.com) and paid tiers are the business. All JavaScript is MIT and GitLab says most EE code is open source.

license_history.note: Original project, completely free and open source

license_history.license: CE: MIT; EE: initially MIT but not published, later the proprietary GitLab EE licence
license_history.note: GitLab 6.0 introduced Enterprise Edition on 22 Aug 2013

license_history.license: CE: MIT; EE: GitLab Enterprise Edition licence (source-available)
license_history.note: Current docs; GitLab describes itself as open-core with source-available proprietary code

relicensing_events.to: Open core: MIT CE + proprietary-licensed EE
relicensing_events.outcome_note: Not a relicense of existing code but the creation of a closed tier; no significant fork. The company grew to ~$1B ARR under this model

exit_events.note: Priced 13 Oct 2021 at $77 (above $66-69 range), ~$801M gross proceeds; ~$11B valuation at IPO price; opened at $94.25 (~$13.5B per Bloomberg)

risk_events: Still GAAP loss-making: FY2026 GAAP operating margin -7% (non-GAAP +17%; $220M adjusted free cash flow)
Stock well below IPO price: ~$45 on 23 Nov 2026 vs $77 IPO; 52-week range $18.73-$58.01
Growth deceleration: FY2027 guidance 15-17% after 26% in FY2026
Founder-CEO transition: Bill Staples is CEO (Sijbrandij remains a director and sold shares in Nov 2026)
Direct competition from Microsoft-owned GitHub, which bundles AI coding tools
robustness: Public company, crossed $1B ARR in FY2026 with positive free cash flow and a $400M buyback authorisation. The MIT-licensed CE means self-hosters and forks could continue without the company, but the product's development is single-vendor (no foundation) and EE features remain proprietary.
physical_science_relevance: Self-hosted GitLab CE is widely used by universities, national labs and research groups that need on-premise code hosting and CI (e.g. for data-sensitive or air-gapped research).
openness_effect_assessment: Openness drove adoption: a free MIT self-hosted alternative to GitHub won universities and enterprises, and open core converted that base into ~$955M revenue (FY2026). The 2013 move to a proprietary enterprise tier caused no damaging fork because the open core stayed genuinely useful. But open core has not protected valuation: the company trades at ~$7.2B, below its ~$11B IPO value, as AI-native competition rises.
key_takeaway: GitLab is a successful example of a community open-source project turned into a public open-core company. It moved from fully open (level 3) to open core (level 2) early and transparently, avoided licence controversies like those of database vendors, and reached ~$1B ARR, yet still competes mainly against a closed, Microsoft-backed rival and remains GAAP-unprofitable.
